name: How Do Change Orders Affect a Kitchen Remodeling Estimate?

mainEntity.name: How should change orders be compared when kitchen remodeling estimates have different rules for unexpected work?
mainEntity.text: How should change orders be compared when kitchen remodeling estimates have different rules for unexpected work?

acceptedAnswer.text: Change-order terms can make two similar estimates produce very different final prices. Ask each contractor how added work is priced, whether labor uses fixed prices or hourly rates, what material markup applies, and whether supervision, delivery, disposal, taxes, or scheduling effects are added. Confirm how credits are calculated when work or materials are removed. The estimate should require a written description of the change, its price impact, schedule impact, and revised completion date before approval. Ask whether emailed or text approvals are accepted and who may authorize them. Clarify how concealed damage, failed inspections, owner-requested upgrades, damaged products, and contractor errors are treated. Homeowners should not pay for correcting work that was included in the original scope or performed improperly. For kitchens in the Tampa Bay area, request examples of common changes such as subfloor repair, electrical upgrades, plumbing relocation, wall repairs, or cabinet filler adjustments. Keep a running change log with the original price, revised price, reason, approval date, and payment status. A clear process protects the budget while allowing legitimate conditions to be resolved without confusion.
acceptedAnswer.description: A change-order clause should explain how added or deleted work is priced, documented, approved, and scheduled. Compare labor rates, material markups, supervision charges, credits, and emergency decisions. Require written approval before nonurgent extra work begins, except where immediate action prevents damage.
